# Proposal 1 · §1–5 Vision → pagination

DESIGN PROPOSAL · PART 1 OF 5 · §1–5

# Linen — an EPUB reader that gets out of the way

A product, UX, interaction, information architecture and extensibility proposal for a calm, cross-platform EPUB reader, desktop and tablet first. “Linen” is a working name. Tags like Screen 03 and S2 point to boards on the Screens and System pages.

#### At a glance — the ten decisions that matter most

- Books open immersive: no permanent chrome.
- Controls appear on an edge, a centre tap or Tab, and hide on the next page turn.
- Pages by default; Scroll is the only alternative.
- One wheel notch or trackpad gesture turns at most one page.
- Contents, Search and Notes share one Navigator sidebar.
- Every jump can be undone through history and a Back chip.
- A highlight is one click, a tint plus an underline; notes live in the margin; Undo instead of dialogs.
- The Aa popover has four controls.
- The publisher decides structure; the reader decides comfort.
- Extensions get slots and permissions, never the page.

#### Revision 2 — after the accessibility and usability review

- Highlights and search marks no longer rely on tint alone: every highlight has a 2 px underline; every search match has an outline; colour names appear in lists.
- Every single-key shortcut has a modified equivalent and can be switched off; chapters also move with ⌥↑ / ⌥↓.
- Night-theme controls, a narrow window, the command palette, the footnote peek and Go to are now drawn Screens 14–17.
- New rules: the visible page follows the screen reader; focus returns to the text after every layer; messages queue and pause; tap priority; OS edge conflicts; Library in the Navigator header.
- Reading sizes corrected to match the screens: 19 px desktop, 20 px tablet.

## 1 Product vision and design principles

**What it is.** Linen is a reader, not a library manager. It opens EPUB files, remembers exactly where you were, and makes hours of reading comfortable on a laptop, monitor or tablet. Conversion, metadata editing, stores and social features are out of scope; anything beyond reading arrives as an extension.

**Problems it solves.** Desktop readers look like document viewers, with toolbars and sidebars competing with the text. Their defaults fail on large screens, where lines run past 120 characters. Input is unreliable: trackpad momentum flips three pages, and a click meant to start a selection turns one. Annotation is missing or buried, and every power feature gets a permanent button.

**How it differs.** Collection managers optimise the minutes spent organising books; Linen optimises the hours spent inside one. A surface earns screen space only while someone is using it.

**Immersion, concretely.** At rest the window shows the page and at most one line of quiet location text: no toolbar, no sidebar, no pointer after two idle seconds, no motion the reader didn’t cause. Controls appear on intent (pointer at the top or bottom edge, a centre tap, Tab) and leave on the next page turn. Nothing — notification, badge or extension UI — appears uninvited. The library, metadata, settings beyond the Aa popover, statistics and extension panels all stay one deliberate step away.

| Principle | Meaning | Concrete consequences |
|---|---|---|
| **Text is the interface** | The page owns the window at rest | No permanent toolbar; chrome overlays the margins instead of resizing the page; books open immersive |
| **Summon, don’t station** | Controls appear where intent is expressed | Edge reveal; selection bar at the selection; Aa popover at its button; footnotes as peeks |
| **One layer at a time** | At most one floating surface over text | Opening search closes the Aa popover; Esc removes exactly one layer S2 |
| **Comfort by default** | Good typography with zero setup | 56–74 character measure, 1.55 line height, paper-toned themes, publisher CSS normalised |
| **Predictable input** | One meaning per gesture per device | A wheel notch or trackpad gesture turns at most one page; clicks in text never turn pages |
| **Progressive depth** | Reading → quick controls → preferences | Four controls in Aa; everything else in Preferences or extensions |
| **Native where it counts** | Follow the OS for windows, menus, keys, files | ⌘ or Ctrl, native context menus, system theme, OS selection handles on touch |
| **Extensions are guests** | Plugins get slots, not the page | Command palette, selection “⋯” menu, Navigator tabs; no DOM access to the reader |

## 2 Target users and usage scenarios

| Group | Typical session | What they need most |
|---|---|---|
| **Long-form reader** — novels, narrative non-fiction | 30–120 min, evenings, often a tablet | Pagination, calm themes, instant resume, zero chrome |
| **Study reader** — academic, technical | 20–60 min at a desk, keyboard | Search, highlights with notes, a reliable way back after a footnote, export later |
| **Documentation reader** — manuals, programming books | Short look-ups between other work | Code and tables that survive, fast search, a scroll mode |
| **Mixed-input reader** — touch laptop, tablet with keyboard | Switches input mid-session | Every action reachable from any input, without a mode switch |

### Core journeys

- **Import or open.** Double-click an .epub, drop it on the window, or press ⌘O. The book opens straight into reading and joins the library as a side effect. Unreadable files get a recoverable error card Screen 12.
- **Start or resume.** Books reopen at the exact saved position (an EPUB CFI); new books open at the first body chapter via the bodymatter landmark, not the cover. Resuming deep in a book shows a four-second chip: “Resumed in Chapter 12 · Go to beginning”.
- **Navigate chapters.** ⌥↓ / ⌥↑ (or ] and [), the Contents tab Screen 04, or the progress scrubber.
- **Search.** ⌘F opens the Navigator’s Search tab, pre-filled with any selection. Esc returns to your page unless you chose a result Screen 05.
- **Select text.** Native selection; on release a compact bar appears above it, never on top of it Screen 06.
- **Highlight or annotate.** One click on a colour saves the highlight. “Note” opens a margin card that saves as you type Screen 07.
- **Adjust typography.** ⌘+ and ⌘− anywhere; the Aa popover for size, theme, spacing and layout Screen 09.
- **Reading ↔ library.** ⌘L or “Library” saves the position. The book leads Continue reading and stays warm in memory, so going back is instant Screen 01.
- **Manage extensions.** Preferences › Extensions shows status and permissions, enables and disables, and installs from a file Screen 11.

## 3 Information architecture

There are two full pages, Library and Reader. Everything else is a layer over the reading canvas S1.

| Surface | Form | Why this form |
|---|---|---|
| Library | Full page | The only place that shows many books |
| Reader | Full page | The product |
| Top and bottom chrome | Transient overlay | Orientation and entry points; gone on the next page turn |
| Navigator: Contents · Search · Notes | Left sidebar, 320 px | All “go somewhere in this book” tasks share one place and one habit; floats as a sheet below 1100 px |
| Reading settings (Aa) | Popover | Four controls don’t justify a panel |
| Go to location | Popover from the progress label | Rare and precise |
| Selection bar, note card, footnote peek, image view | Contextual, anchored to text | Appear where you’re reading, leave with the task |
| Command palette | Modal, ⌘K | Long-tail and extension commands without new buttons |
| Book info | Sheet | Rarely needed while reading |
| Preferences, incl. Extensions | Own window; sheet on tablet | Configuring is not reading |

**Keeping context.** The reader is never unloaded while layers are open. On wide windows the Navigator docks and the column recentres in the remaining space without reflowing; on narrow windows it floats. Every jump — contents entry, search result, link, annotation, percentage — pushes the previous location onto a history stack, so Back (⌘[ / Alt+←) always returns. Leaving for the library writes the position immediately.

## 4 Reader interface: the reading canvas

| Property | Default and rule |
|---|---|
| Measure | Target 66 characters, clamped to 56–74 (CJK 34–40). Set in ch of the current font, so it follows font size. |
| Font size | 19 px desktop, 20 px tablet, scaled by the OS text size; 12 steps from 14 to 32 px, up to 48 px with ⌘+. |
| Line height | 1.55 (Compact 1.4, Loose 1.75); +0.05 automatically above 70 characters per line. |
| Paragraphs | Keep the book’s convention (indent or spacing); if it has neither, add 0.8 em between paragraphs. |
| Alignment | Follow the book; justified text only with hyphenation on, otherwise rivers form. |
| Margins | Sides take what the measure leaves: (W − measure) / 2, never under 24 px desktop, 32 px tablet, 20 px phone. Top and bottom max(48 px, 7vh) S3. |
| Themes | Paper #F7F3EC / #22201C (14.7:1) · Sepia #F1E6D2 / #3B2F22 (10.5:1) · Night #1B1A18 / #D9D3C7 (11.7:1) · Auto follows the system between Paper and Night. No pure white or black: glare and halation build up over long sessions Screen 10. |
| Images at Night | Dimmed about 10%, never inverted. |

**Responsive behaviour.** The column is min(measure, W − 2 × min margin). Extra width becomes margin, never longer lines; from 1480 px, Pages mode shows a two-page spread. Height sets the page, snapped to whole lines so no half line is cut; below 480 px the location line goes. Larger font sizes widen the column until it meets the minimum margins; after that, characters per line fall, because legibility at large sizes beats an ideal measure. Portrait tablets show one column; landscape shows one column with generous margins, and a spread only when two full measures fit. Tablets get 1 px more text, wider margins for thumbs and tap zones; desktops get margin click targets.

**Reflow.** Any change of size, font or theme re-paginates around an anchor — the first visible character’s CFI — so you never lose the line you were on. Resizing is debounced by 120 ms and reflows only the current chapter live; the rest is recomputed when idle.

## 5 Reading modes and pagination

| Mode | Strengths | Weaknesses | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paginated (CSS columns) | Stable spatial memory, no line creep, exact positions, natural for keys and taps | Tables and code can split; reflow cost on huge chapters | **Default** |
| Continuous scroll | Natural for documentation, code and wide tables; smooth on trackpads | Easy to lose your place; weaker spatial memory | The one alternative |
| Horizontal slide | Spatial continuity while a finger drags the page | Visual noise when triggered by keys | Touch swipes only |
| Page curl | Nostalgia | Slow and distracting | Never |

**Recommendation:** Pages by default, Scroll as the only alternative, chosen in the Aa popover and remembered per book. Both modes share anchors, so switching keeps your place. When more than 30% of a book is code or tables, the Aa popover shows a one-line hint to try Scroll — nothing more intrusive.

| Input | Pages | Scroll |
|---|---|---|
| Mouse wheel (notched) | One notch = one page; 250 ms cooldown | Native scrolling |
| Trackpad, two fingers, vertical | Distance accumulates; one turn at 80 px, then locked until the gesture and its momentum end | Native, with momentum |
| Trackpad, two fingers, horizontal | One turn per swipe; content follows the fingers, respecting natural scrolling | Ignored |
| ← → · Space ⇧Space · PgDn PgUp · ↓ ↑ | Next / previous page | A screen at a time with two lines of overlap; ↓ ↑ scroll by line |
| Touch swipe | Finger-tracked; commits past 30% of the width or on a flick | Native scrolling |
| Touch tap | Zones 30 / 40 / 30: back · controls · forward Screen 13. A tap on a link, note marker or highlight always wins over the zones. | Centre tap toggles controls |

**Preventing accidental turns.** A gesture’s axis is locked by its first 12 px of travel, so a diagonal swipe can’t both turn and scroll. Detection works on accumulated distance, not event counts, so high-resolution trackpads behave like ordinary ones. After a turn, momentum is ignored — through gesture phases on macOS, and on Windows precision touchpads by detecting steadily decaying deltas. Nothing turns during a selection drag, and the click that activates an inactive window never turns a page. Rapid input queues at most one pending turn, and neighbouring pages are pre-laid out so a turn renders within a frame. If more than three pages pass in under a second, a “Back to page 41” chip offers a way back.

**RTL and vertical writing.** The spine’s page-progression-direction decides direction. In RTL books ← is the next page, the left tap zone moves forward, swipes mirror and progress fills right to left; arrow keys stay spatial, as in Apple Books and Kindle. Vertical text (writing-mode: vertical-rl) paginates right to left with ruby preserved; Scroll becomes horizontal for these books, but Pages stays the recommendation.
